hops.title: Seattle crows remembered the mask
hops.text: In 2006 at the University of Washington, John Marzluff wore a fearsome mask to trap, band and release seven wild crows. Researchers also walked campus in a neutral mask, a likeness of Dick Cheney, and left the birds alone. For years afterward, crows scolded people in the trapping mask more often than people in the Cheney mask. Uncaught crows and their young joined in. On one walk, 47 of 53 crows scolded the trapping face, and the scolding spread over a kilometer. In a separate experiment, crows stared, frozen, at a mask they had learned to link with capture; scans taken afterward showed raised activity in an amygdala region.

sources.citation: University of Washington Urban@UW News. Crows hold grudges against individual humans for up to 17 years.

hops.afterHeading: The key experiment: cutting one route at a time
hops.title: Playing possum is two responses, not one
hops.text: Playing possum looks like a single act: the animal lies still and looks dead. Telemetry on four free-ranging American opossums shows two responses running at once. After vigorous contact from a person or dog, the opossums lay stiff with their mouths open; heart rate fell 46 percent and breathing 30 percent, and their hearts slowed again when the dog came back, so they were still tracking it. When researchers gave atropine, which blocks the nerve signal that slows the heart, the heart-rate drop vanished, but the rigid posture stayed. The drug separated the two responses, much as the rat lesions separate freezing from the rise in blood pressure.

sources.citation: Gabrielsen, G. W., & Smith, E. N. (1985). Physiological responses associated with feigned death in the American opossum. Acta Physiologica Scandinavica, 123(4), 393–398.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An American opossum lying motionless on forest leaves while a puzzled dog sniffs nearby.
image.caption: A drug can block an opossum's slowed heart while its stiff, motionless pose carries on.

hops.afterHeading: The slow route: the HPA loop
hops.title: A century of whale cortisol in earwax
hops.text: In the Smithsonian and London's Natural History Museum sit long plugs of earwax from fin, humpback and blue whales. Baleen whales build up earwax in bands like tree rings, and each band preserves cortisol from about six months of the whale's life. Biologists measured 1,084 bands from 20 earplugs, from museums and stranded whales, spanning 1870 to 2016. Scored against each whale's own baseline, cortisol peaked at 68 percent above it in the early 1960s, at the height of industrial whaling. During World War II, when whaling fell, the score still rose 10 percent; the authors suspect naval activity contributed.

sources.citation: Trumble, S. J., Robinson, E. M., Berman-Kowalewski, M., Potter, C. W., & Usenko, S. (2013). Blue whale earplug reveals lifetime contaminant exposure and hormone profiles. PNAS, 110(42), 16922–16926.

Trumble, S. J., Norman, S. A., Crain, D. D., Mansouri, F., Winfield, Z. C., Sabin, R., Potter, C. W., Gabriele, C. M., & Usenko, S. (2018). Baleen whale cortisol levels reveal a physiological response to 20th century whaling. Nature Communications, 9, 4587.

image.caption: Each band of whale earwax holds about six months of cortisol, a record that tracks the whaling era.

audio.title: Grudge-holding crows, whale earwax and tickled rats
audio.transcript:
Here are three true stories about learned reactions, stress hormones and what animal behavior can tell us.

The first starts in two thousand six at the University of Washington. Biologist John Marzluff pulled on a fearsome mask, trapped seven wild American crows, put bands on their legs and let them go. To test whether the birds were reacting to any masked human or only to the dangerous face, researchers also walked across campus in a neutral mask, a likeness of the then Vice President, Dick Cheney, and fed the crows without bothering them. For years afterward, crows were more likely to scold people in the trapping mask than people in the Cheney mask. Crows that had never been caught, and young birds hatched later, picked up the grudge from their neighbors. On one walk, forty-seven of fifty-three crows scolded the trapping mask. By September twenty twenty-three, seventeen years after the trapping began, Marzluff went on one masked walk without hearing a single scold. In a separate experiment, crows froze and stared at a face they had learned to associate with capture, and brain scans taken afterward showed higher activity in regions including the amygdala, thalamus and brainstem. Like the tone in the rat experiment, the trapping mask had become a signal for danger.

Now move from the fast circuits to the slow hormone route, the H P A axis. The adrenal cortex releases cortisol into the blood, and in baleen whales some of it ends up preserved in long, layered plugs of earwax. A fin, humpback or blue whale builds up that wax in bands, like tree rings, and each band holds cortisol from about six months of its life. Biologists analyzed more than a thousand of those bands from twenty earplugs, some archived at the Smithsonian and London's Natural History Museum and some from stranded whales, covering the years eighteen seventy to twenty sixteen. They scored each band against that whale's own baseline. The average score peaked in the early nineteen sixties, at the height of industrial whaling, at sixty-eight percent above baseline. And during World War Two, when commercial whaling fell sharply, the score still rose about ten percent. The researchers suspect that wartime activity at sea, from naval battles to underwater explosions, may have contributed.

Finally, if freezing does not tell us directly what a rat feels, what about the other end of emotion? In two thousand, Jaak Panksepp and Jeffrey Burgdorf reported that young rats tickled by an experimenter emit fifty-kilohertz ultrasonic chirps, far too high for human ears, and that rats housed alone quickly learn to chirp at a cue that predicts tickling. In twenty sixteen, another lab showed that tickled rats chase the hand and make little unsolicited hops, with activity in touch-cortex neurons that tracks the tickling and is suppressed when the rat is put in an anxious setting. It is hard not to smile at a chirping, hopping rat. Yet Panksepp put a question mark right after the word laughter in his paper's title. Whether a rat freezes at a tone or chirps at a tickle, the response gives researchers something to measure. Learning what the rat feels takes more than that measurement.
